title: Precinct of Mut
summary: The precinct of the goddess Mut south of Karnak: her temple almost ringed by the crescent-shaped Isheru lake, the lion-headed Sekhmet statues of Amenhotep III, Temple A, the temple of Ramesses III and Taharqa’s gate.
orientation: About 100 yards (90 m) south of the precinct of Amun, linked to it by an avenue of sphinxes from the Tenth Pylon.

claims.text: The Isheru surrounds Mut’s temple on three sides and belongs to the distinctive sacred landscape of Eye-of-Re goddesses.
Temple A and the Ramesses III temple entered the enclosure through later expansions; they were not all originally inside one boundary.

claims.text: Excavations west of the Taharqa Gate exposed older paving below later Ptolemaic occupation, illustrating changes in circulation and use.

caveats: This is not the Ramesses III bark temple in the Amun Great Court.

sections.heading: Where you are
paragraphs: The precinct of Mut lies about 100 yards (90 m) south of the temple of Amun and faces it; an avenue of sphinxes links the two. Mut was Amun’s wife and, with their son Khonsu, formed the Theban triad.

The precinct reopened to the public in January 2014 after being closed for almost 40 years, following work by the Brooklyn Museum and Johns Hopkins University expeditions and the American Research Center in Egypt.

sections.heading: The temple of Mut and the Isheru
paragraphs: The temple of Mut is surrounded on three sides by a crescent-shaped sacred lake, the Isheru. A temple to Mut may have stood here as early as the Middle Kingdom, and the Johns Hopkins expedition found evidence of an earlier temple below the later building, but the earliest standing remains date to Hatshepsut and Thutmose III. Until the 25th Dynasty the precinct held only the temple of Mut and its lake.
look: The curve of the Isheru around the back of the temple.

sections.heading: The Sekhmet statues
paragraphs: Amenhotep III filled the precinct with seated and standing granite statues of the lion-headed goddess Sekhmet, a fierce form linked with Mut at Thebes; one estimate puts their original number at about 570. Most seem to have been made for this site, though some may have come from Amenhotep III’s mortuary temple on the west bank.
Many still stand in the courts and along the Isheru. Others were taken to museums: the British Museum alone has about thirty and the Egyptian Museum in Cairo six.
look: The seated Sekhmet statues still standing in the courts and beside the lake.

sections.heading: Temple A
paragraphs: In the north-east corner stands the building known as Temple A. A block from it names a “Temple of Millions of Years” of Ramesses II. It lay outside the precinct until Taharqa brought it inside in the 25th Dynasty, and by the Third Intermediate Period it served as a birth house, a temple celebrating the divine birth of a god.

citations.locator: Block naming a Temple of Millions of Years of Ramesses II

sections.heading: The temple of Ramesses III
paragraphs: South-west of the Isheru stands a temple of Ramesses III, which was also outside the precinct at first. In the 1920s Maurice Pillet cleared it and re-erected the two colossal statues of the king in front of its entrance.

sections.heading: Taharqa’s gate and the final walls
paragraphs: Taharqa built a gate in a new western enclosure wall, opening a processional way to Temple A; it is carved with scenes of his divine birth and his acceptance by the gods. The precinct reached its final size in the 4th century BC, when either Nectanebo II or an early Ptolemy added the monumental entrance, the propylon, and built massive walls around Temple A, the Ramesses III temple and the area south of the Isheru. The Taharqa gate was then blocked; the Brooklyn expedition rebuilt it in 2008–2009.
On the propylon a Ptolemaic king and two priestesses play music before the goddesses.
look: The music-making scene on the propylon at the entrance.

questions.text: How far did a Middle Kingdom temple of Mut extend? Only traces below the later temple are known.
